messages.subject: Re: Standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Robert,

No doubt someone has made recommendations regarding the magnitude of SEs, though I'm not sure how much value they would be in practice. You could use SEs for hypothesis testing purposes w.r.t. whether a new item should be included in a test battery, but in general I would advise against that as there are more important issues in that context than whether a discrimination is "significant" in the conventional sense. Mainly, I would use the SE information to help safeguard against over interpretation of a test item's discrimination capabilities as large SEs result in wide CIs, so an ostensibly large discrimination could simply be due to sampling uncertainty, and it's worthwhile to know that. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Milica,

The default constraint method in DIF() is the 'add' scheme, which adds equality constraints to create the nested model structure for testing. In this case items Q10 and Q30 already had their parameters and subsequent estimates constrained to be equal as they are anchors, so there's no additional constraint additions to be made. You could, however, test whether the anchors themselves contain DIF using the 'drop' approach, though you do run the risk of losing empirical identification if the model isn't sufficiently constrained to do so (2 items for anchoring is close to the bare minimum....). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Reverse Direction of Item Coefficients in Unidimensional and Multidimensional Graded Response Models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gerry,

You're fitting an exploratory IRT model, so the initial extracted solution is generally not interpretable as it's a solution based on maximum extraction principles instead of fitting some precise, confirmatory-like model. You can find information about this in the traditional linear exploratory factor analysis literature, where extracted solutions are effectively arbitrary and should be rotated to something that is conceptually more useful given the covariation patterns. HTH.

Phil

Hi Oxana,

On Sun, Aug 25, 2024 at 10:53 PM Oxana Rosca <oxan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Phil,
>
> Thank you for the mirt package and your informative responses.
>
> I've got similar results but without group comparison. I work with multistage testing reading assessment that was developed for high-school students. My sample was 4,500 undergraduate students, and the assessment seemed expectedly easy for them. The item pool consisted of 30 6-item passages/testlets. Each student responded to 3 randomly chosen passages (18 items). Every passage was responded to by 400-500 students. The boxplot of mean values in the attached file shows that three-quarters of 180 items were responded to correctly by 75% or more of the students who got them. However, all but one location parameter (b-parameter or d-parameter) estimated by the bifactor 2PL model are positive. The 169 items ranged from  -0.08 to 5.98 (the theta scale is -6, 6). Eleven items had location parameters between 6 and 18.6.

The d parameters are intercepts, not the traditional difficulty parameter (b), so in that sense they are more akin to "easiness" parameters centered at the value when theta = 0 (cf. b values, which reflect the theta location where the response curve inflects, which is often at P(theta) = .5). So a number of high values makes sense in this context and indeed reflects the easiness of the item. If it helps, mirt has an interactive shiny interface to get accustomed to the parameterisations, which can be loaded via mirt::itemplot(shiny=TRUE)

>
> As I understand, such results suggest that the assessment was hard for the sample. Please help me with this puzzle.
>
> My second question is about the a2-parameters (for specific factors/testlets). You mentioned in your other responses in this group that negative a2-parameters were OK since they are calculated as partial correlation coefficients via regression. You also mentioned that a-parameters with absolute values smaller than 0.1 could be excluded from the assessments because their inflection point is very far from the center of theta distribution, hence, they are too difficult for all respondents of the sample. Does the latter apply to a1-parameters and/or a2-parameters of the bifactor model?

In the context of a bifactor model the a2 parameter being small would indicate a weak partial correlation, so the specific factor has little influence over an item. In such cases you could consider dropping the loading as they would be unlikely to influence the measurement model's results. Note that small a's are not 'difficulty', they are just not very informative as the item is not really influence by changes in the defined latent trait (at least, as far as it is able to tell within the predictable scope of the model). HTH.

Phil

It's somewhat semantics. IRT is factor analysis of categorical data, where classical versions of IRT are basically some version of one factor models with various response functions. Sometimes the FA models with special link functions will match the response models found in IRT, such as the 2PL and GRM.

>
> Are the CFA models (single group & multiple group) estimated by mirt the same or comparable to those estimated by Mplus or lavaan? What can I do to make the mirt output as similar to Mplus output as possible? I mean the choice of the estimation method, etc.

If you use the weighted likelihood estimators in lavaan/Mplus for categorical response variables you'll obtain limited information estimates of specific types of IRT models that assume ordinal responses. Might be worthwhile to read an article or two on this, such as the following:

Wirth, R. & Edwards, M. C.
Item factor analysis: Current approaches and future directions.
Psychological Methods, American Psychological Association, 2007, 12, 58-79

Dear Dr. Chalmers,

Thank you for your exceptional work and support. I have developed a Computerized Adaptive Test (CAT) that ensures content balance. Prior to implementing the CAT, I propose administering a linear exam to students. This exam will include items from each content area, with specific constraints on parameters (a) and (b). Based on the theta values obtained from this linear exam, the actual CAT will proceed, maintaining content area balance.

Could you advise on the best method to initialize theta for the CAT code and remove the items selected for the initial linear exam from the item bank?

test_properties <- data.frame(content=rep(c('ContentArea1', 'ContentArea2', 'ContentArea3','ContentArea4','ContentArea5'),
                                          times=60),skills=rep(c('Skill1', 'Skill2', 'Skill3'), times = 100))
head(test_properties)
test_properties
# Create the item bank as a data frame
# constraint generating function
constr_fun <- function(person, test, design) {
  mo <- extract.mirtCAT(test, 'mo')
  # Get the number of items from the test object
  nitems <- extract.mirt(mo, 'nitems')

  # Access the content labels (assuming they're stored in tp$content or similar)
  tp <- extract.mirtCAT(design, 'test_properties')  # Assuming the test object contains a 'tp' element with content info

  lhs <- matrix(0, nrow = 14, ncol = nitems)  # 5 content areas with min/max + 1 total

  # Add constraints based on content labels
  lhs[1, tp$content == 'ContentArea1'] <- 1  # Min items from ContentArea1
  lhs[2, tp$content == 'ContentArea1'] <- 1  # Max items from ContentArea1

  lhs[3, tp$content == 'ContentArea2'] <- 1  # Min items from ContentArea2
  lhs[4, tp$content == 'ContentArea2'] <- 1  # Max items from ContentArea2

  lhs[5, tp$content == 'ContentArea3'] <- 1  # Min items from ContentArea3
  lhs[6, tp$content == 'ContentArea3'] <- 1  # Max items from ContentArea3

  lhs[7, tp$content == 'ContentArea4'] <- 1  # Min items from ContentArea4
  lhs[8, tp$content == 'ContentArea4'] <- 1  # Max items from ContentArea4

  lhs[9, tp$content == 'ContentArea5'] <- 1  # Min items from ContentArea5
  lhs[10, tp$content == 'ContentArea5'] <- 1 # Max items from ContentArea5

  lhs[11, tp$skill == 'Skill1'] <- 1
  lhs[12, tp$skill == 'Skill2'] <- 1
  lhs[13, tp$skill == 'Skill3'] <- 1

  # Constraint for total number of items (row 11)
  lhs[14, ] <- 1  # All items contribute to the total number of items

  # Specify the relationship direction for each constraint
  dirs <- c(">=", "<=",  # Min and max for ContentArea1
            ">=", "<=",  # Min and max for ContentArea2
            ">=", "<=",  # Min and max for ContentArea3
            ">=", "<=",  # Min and max for ContentArea4
            ">=", "<=",  # Min and max for ContentArea5
            ">=",">=",">=", # Min for each skill
            "<=")        # Total number of items

  # Specify the right-hand side (RHS) of the constraints
  rhs <- c(5, 15,  # Min 5, max 15 for ContentArea1
           5, 15,  # Min 5, max 15 for ContentArea2
           5, 15,  # Min 5, max 15 for ContentArea3
           5, 15,  # Min 5, max 15 for ContentArea4
           5, 15,
           5,5,5,# Min 5, max 15 for ContentArea5
           40)     # Total items <= 20

  # Return the constraints as a data frame
  constraints <- data.frame(lhs, dirs, rhs)
  constraints
}

# next item selection function
customNextItem <- function(person, design, test){
  objective <- computeCriteria(person=person, design=design, test=test,
                               criteria = 'MI')
  item <- findNextItem(person=person, design=design, test=test,
                       objective=objective)
  item
}

  max_items = 40, min_SEM = 0.3
)
